column2: The Before section's catalogue of claimed pre-event reconnaissance — campus layouts, legal actors, medical staff, people in Charlie's orbit. Retrospective pattern-matching is the risk the page names on itself.
The censorship section's record of vanishing graphs: campus scout terms, case names, and the archives researchers keep because live results shift. This is framed as record loss, not merely ranking.
Readers who already know this site exists report struggling to find it again through Google. The page sets the suppression reading and the ordinary algorithmic one side by side.

A defamation suit that puts the man who was in the SUV and the most prominent independent voice on the case on opposite sides of a courtroom — with a reported mass recusal of an entire district's judges. Nothing in it is a court finding yet.
Counter-UAS testing at Provo airport the same week, fast objects on phone video, and TPUSA later acknowledging drone use. Airspace is treated here as evidence rather than as a sideshow.
Federal posture, ballistics stewardship, witness coordination and the press briefings — plus the open questions that make disclosure the point. The bureau is a subject here, not a source.

Four federal laws modelled on the Epstein Files Transparency Act, plus reform plans for evidence handling and event security. This is where subscriber identities behind a geography bucket would actually be compelled into view.

The Egyptian president met the CENTCOM commander two days before the killing — a routine, publicly logged meeting that some threads restage as a shadow timeline. This page keeps the proximity and refuses the inference, then holds the "Admiral Cooper" image-search claim to the same standard.

A Navy contract for miniaturized demolition charges, delivered sixteen days before the assassination, is the only hard document in this thread. It is also still public and still searchable — which cuts against the suppression story it is cited to support.

Washington appears in these threads as shorthand for federal attention: the receiving hospital on June 28, July 3 and July 16, then again the day before the shooting. Virginia is context here, not a dataset, and the page says so plainly.

DIA enters this case institutionally rather than evidentially — through Fort Huachuca and a defense-intelligence portfolio, never through a document. That is a reason to demand disclosure, not a finding.
Utah's law-enforcement leadership turned over twice in the summer before the killing, and both incoming names sit inside the search claims. Mehtab Syed on July 9, Robert Bohls on September 1.

The claim is that named people vanished from image search overnight while unnamed people stayed — a control test run once, by the interested party, with no archived before-state. The innocent explanation is that a person asked Google to remove their own photographs.

A former Army OPSEC instructor argues junior soldiers routinely image-search VIPs before escorting them onto post — so the claimed anomaly is not the searching but who was searched, and when. The reported cluster runs from mid-July to the morning of September 9.

The router for the whole section, and the only page that puts the methodology limits ahead of the claims. Aggregate geography is not a list of searchers, and post-event hindsight makes any earlier spike look predictive.

The largest bucket in this research is a Trends country filter, not a list of workstations — and the page concedes that in its first paragraph. What survives is a dated list running from August 2024 campus layouts to a September 1 FBI name.

The claim is not that the judges were searched. It is that Utah reportedly did not search them at all until after Charlie Kirk died, while a foreign geography did months earlier — Lunnen in May, Graf in July.

One midsummer week carries the AMFEST Tucker Carlson booking, an Egyptian jet's reported first American trip, a new Utah DPS commissioner and a two-week surgeon search frenzy. Commentators use it as a synchrony anchor, not a proven planning date.

A one-week surge in December 2024 for a Utah defense attorney — nine months before there was a case for her to defend. The page keeps the timing question and refuses the accusation: court-appointed capital counsel is a routine process.

The names that get lost inside screenshot dumps — a future jailhouse informant reportedly searched back in November 2023, a paving contractor, a domain nobody yet had a reason to care about. Indexed so researchers do not lose them.

The strongest available version of the Trends argument: not a screenshot, but a screenshot you can reproduce on demand. That answers the cherry-picking objection and nothing else — a spike to 100 can still be a handful of queries.

The hub for every claimed pre-September-10 search pattern, split by geography and by date. It carries the fight over method as well as the data — investigators publishing screenshots on one side, statisticians calling it sampled noise on the other.

Tail numbers are the highest-specificity search term in this whole section — nobody types N1098L by accident. The claimed spike lands 32 days before the shooting; the innocent reading is ADS-B hobbyists.

Seven surgeons, a medical examiner two weeks into the job, and the hospital that would receive Charlie Kirk — all reportedly searched inside a single fortnight in July. This is the claim set with the most names and dates attached to it.

Charlie Kirk's inner circle and the Utah political figures around the event, grouped into the July–August window. Presence in a Trends list is not an accusation, and the page repeats that before every table.

A researcher reports seeing a spike on mobile, zero on desktop, then nothing anywhere — framed as live deletion, equally explained by a UI bug or thin volume. If pre-event search data ever mattered, preservation mattered more.

The accused and his partner appear in more Trends compilations than any other names, with a St. George address claimed under continuous interest from December 2024. Search spikes prove nothing about either of them.

Rooftop, parking, CCTV, layout, Losee Center — the campus strings the whole reconnaissance theory is built on, claimed from August 2024 onward. UVU is also a large public campus with perpetual organic search interest.
Three models of control — behavioural, narrative, and physical frame — graded by evidence rather than argued. If a device rather than a round killed Charlie Kirk, no rooftop shooter of any name did.
The broadcaster behind the Fort Huachuca image-search claims and much of the 2026 coverage of this case. Both July 2026 claim pages in this section originate on his show.
The OSINT account most credited for the Israeli-IP Trends set — the medical examiner, the receiving hospital, and the contractor who paved the courtyard. All attributed, none of it verified.
The site's principal skeptic on this entire section: Trends is sampled noise, unreproducible, and not a historical record at single-digit volumes. Read him against every screenshot here.

The Israel section's own version of the Trends file — legal actors, medical staff, campus layouts and addresses, every item carried as an attributed claim. Aggregate interest identifies no user and no intent.

If Israel is treated as the suspect, why is Israeli software extracting the evidence? The sharpest answer on the page is that the defense, which has every incentive, is not challenging the Cellebrite extraction.
How Robinson's capital defense team was appointed, and what public commentary has claimed about the timing of it. Appointing specialised counsel in a death-penalty case is standard Utah practice.

A surgeon reportedly stepped out of the ER to make a call, and agents reportedly kept him out until told to stand down. The Washington thread running through this page is the same one the search claims lean on.

The medical version of the search claim — examiner, hospital and surgeons reportedly queried from abroad before September 10. If it holds, the significance sits in the pattern and never in any doctor's conduct.

The theory that the lavalier microphone on Charlie Kirk's shirt, not a rooftop round, was the kill mechanism. Shirt fabric reportedly moves spherically before the wound appears, and the audio reportedly splits one event into two.

The motive frameworks that require capability rather than grievance — policy stakes, surveillance aircraft, contractor movements, and a foreign-interference probe reportedly shut down. No court has attributed the killing to any service.
The Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence. The page records his public office and résumé.

Utah's chief medical examiner, weeks into the job when the case arrived, and the name at the centre of the June 30 search claim. Her autopsy report reached the court through another agent, not from the stand.
The student who asked Charlie Kirk the last question of his life, moments before the shooting. Commentary has raised questions about him; the page answers with documented facts only.

Robinson's lead capital defense attorney, thirty years into a criminal-defense career, and the name at the centre of the December 2024 spike claim. The page states plainly that Trends cannot show who searched.
Tyler Robinson's partner and roommate, a cooperating witness, and the source of the messages the state's case leans on. She has not been charged with any crime.

The FBI agent who took over Salt Lake City about a month before the shooting and led the September 11 press conference. Taking over a field office is routine; the timing is what researchers keep listing.
An Army ISR jet on the HADES program flew low, slow passes near UVU before and after the shooting. No track, tasking order or sensor product from it has appeared in the prosecution.
A Special Air Mission callsign for tail 99-0404, reported leaving Fort Huachuca at 0:49 on September 9. Until a flight log is produced it stays an open identifier rather than a manifest.

The Egyptian Falcon 7X reported on the ground near Provo from September 4 to the morning of September 10 — the aircraft Candace Owens called the yellow plane. Its reported first American trip lands in the same July week.

Roughly a dozen lieutenant colonels on base September 8, a VIP flight out the next morning, and a passenger identification no manifest confirms. The organizational overlap with N1098L is real; any tasking is not established.
Callsign AXEL10, extremely low and extremely slow over Orem, before and after 12:23 PM. It very likely did not launch drones; who planned for it to be there is the open question.
Confession messages timestamped 7:57 PM against a phone reportedly seized at Miranda around 6:25 PM, 260 miles away. The page documents the timing conflict without asserting that anything was forged.
The founder of the firm reportedly guarding Charlie Kirk at UVU, and a living private citizen who denies the speculation about him and has sued over related claims.

The firm on the detail that day was reportedly not the one used at earlier Kirk events, and reportedly carried no bodycams. Who was actually standing inside the white shirts is still an open question.
The organisation behind the tour: its structure, donors, security arrangements and internal politics in Charlie Kirk's final weeks. The page does not claim TPUSA is responsible for anything.

The ground where Charlie Kirk died was reportedly stripped of roughly ten inches of soil and paved within days, on a deadline the contractor attributes to the governor and the FBI. It is the primary trace surface of the homicide.
Almost everything researchers claim from 2024 is a single evidence class: Trends screenshots. The page says that first, then lists the August campus searches and the December spike anyway.

The whole pressure arc of 2025 in order — donor and policy friction, TPUSA internal politics, foreign aircraft, and the private messages researchers treat as pressure points. The July anchor week sits inside it.
The hypothesis that someone was watching Robinson's online activity months before the shooting — and the query strings researchers cite as the trace. Unverified without primary documents.

A compressed 36-hour window at the Army's intelligence schoolhouse — a reported closed-door meeting, a VIP jet, and a walk-in witness who says he was detained and questioned. None of it appears in the state's case.

The NCTC director who says on the record that his parallel foreign-ties review was halted before its leads were exhausted. NCTC stops only once foreign ties are ruled out — and by his account they never were.

A month after Charlie Kirk died, the Tennessee plant that makes shaped charges and demolition blocks was destroyed, reportedly killing sixteen workers. Industrial explosions have ordinary causes; investigators still want the timeline explained.
The Israeli forensics firm named in open court as the tool that pulled Lance Twiggs' phone. Confirmed by testimony — which is more than any Trends screenshot in this section can say.
The judge whose August 2025 retirement created the vacancy Tony Graf filled weeks before the case arrived. He had no involvement in it — the interest is entirely in the sequence.

The judge presiding over State v. Robinson, sworn in weeks before the shooting, in what commentary calls his first case on the bench. Appointment timing is an open question in posts, not a court finding.

The Utah DPS commissioner appointed weeks before the assassination, and the official who cleared George Zinn the same day and locked the weapon class early. His appointment date sits one day after a claimed DC search spike.

A jailhouse informant with no known connection to the case, moved into the same story by a transport order from the bench. Commentators read it as a distraction layer; the page keeps to process facts.
A Utah public figure who gave an early account of where the shot came from, differing from others present. Differing first impressions of a sudden, chaotic event indicate nothing by themselves.
The tracker for gag orders, sealed transcripts, chain-of-custody fights and the discovery commentators say has not arrived. Any search record would have to come through exactly this machinery.
Every map on this site is anchored to one point — the tent. The geometry drawn out from there is what drives the cause-of-death analysis.

State of Utah v. Tyler Robinson: the docket, the change of presiding judge, the December gag order, and the fight over ATF and FBI files. Prosecutors wrote that they do not intend to offer evidence from the seized electronics.
The courtyard where Charlie Kirk was killed was reportedly resurfaced within days, by a company reportedly revived months earlier. UVU says the work was prescheduled. Both accounts are on the page.

The sheriff who took the tip and arranged the surrender, then resigned with no stated reason. The government's own document records that the clothing Robinson arrived in did not match the surveillance clothing.

Six campus officers for an event with a documented threat history, and rooftops treated as outside the detail's jurisdiction. A pre-event email through the chief's chain the day before is a documented item researchers want disclosed.

Court proceedings, sealed evidence, gag orders and the multi-agency investigation — plus the Panguitch alibi claim that restaurant staff say neither side ever tested. The whole apparatus rests on a rifle account the independent analysis disputes.

Government police and prosecutors — not the Bureau — controlled the first custody chain, the crime-scene ground and the state prosecution. Six agencies, one timeline, and the places where their accounts do not line up.

A deliberate pointer page. It marks only the three places federal conduct touches the state and local chain — custody transfer, scene control and discovery — and sends the rest to the Bureau's own section.

The map of this section — who was on scene, who took custody, who paved the courtyard, and where the local accounts conflict. Federal Bureau material is deliberately kept out of it and pointed to instead.
Orem PD sent UVU the ticket link a week before the event, then said afterwards it was "not involved." The joint public-order unit UVU pays for every year was never activated.
Federal agents secured the scene about thirteen minutes after the first call. What the Bureau and the Utah agencies then agreed about witness access is the part no released document covers.

The state's most visible law-enforcement voice in the first forty-eight hours. He announced the recovered rifle and released the enhanced suspect stills — some of them, timeline analysts argue, after a surrender was already being arranged.

The former UVU officer reported to be first onto the Losee Center roof, and the witness whose body-camera recording stopped there. His preliminary-hearing testimony is where the screwdriver enters the record.

A ledger of what officials said and when, including the custody announcement made at 4:21 PM and corrected at 5:59. Reading them side by side is how you separate ordinary first-day error from something else.

The state's own account of its investigation, laid out so it can be checked: the minute-by-minute of September 10, the agencies, the evidence categories and the corrections. The ATF comparison on the recovered fragment came back inconclusive.

A witness says he sent the FBI his close-range footage and was then asked to delete it, with a follow-up call to confirm. A second thread concerns free trauma counselling offered to UVU witnesses. Both are recorded as unverified allegations.

A Texas sheriff's captain, a retired highway patrolman, a Past Master Mason and a funeral director — reportedly the father of the man who founded the firm on the detail. Every one of those is a lawful occupation, and the page says so before it says anything else.

The vendor who says he was "stabbed in the back" when another firm took over the Kirk detail, in an account that lines up with an AP report of last-minute rehiring. His own statement that his company had not worked with TPUSA since 2022 is what makes the white-shirt footage a question.

Anonymous posts claim there was no security plan for the September 11 stop — the event Charlie Kirk never reached. The page keeps it unverified on purpose: a missing plan would speak to preparedness, not to foreknowledge.

The firm that guarded earlier Kirk stops, founded by a reported twenty-year FBI veteran, and reportedly not on the detail that day. A since-deleted post from its own account is the document the whole vendor-switch argument turns on.

A Discord message saying "it was me, all by myself" that reportedly appeared about ninety minutes after custody — and reached the public as photographs of a roommate's phone screen, not an authenticated account export. No signed, sworn confession exists.

A placeholder, and honest about being one. The claim is that an unusual share of the people in the UVU courtyard had Army Military Intelligence ties; until a denominator, a numerator and a baseline exist, a high ratio is an impression rather than a measurement.

The allegation is not that one suspect was charged. It is that the foreign and accomplice lanes were reportedly closed at the same time, with a counterterrorism inquiry into foreign ties halted before its leads were run down.

The domestic-assistance layer of the case: the microphone and its defense contract, the explosives plant destroyed a month later, and the reported closing of the foreign-nexus inquiry. Capability, presence and control, read in that order.

A commercially ordinary wireless lavalier, reportedly worn under the shirt on a magnetic clasp, which researchers trace back to a defense supply chain. The procurement claims attached to it are the part a reader can actually check against award data.

Cement over the courtyard, a transport vehicle reportedly destroyed, a withheld surrender video, and a foreign-involvement inquiry reportedly shut within days. Every item is an allegation; the argument is about the sequence they arrived in.

The plain-English demand behind Law 1, written before any drafting: every DOJ, FBI, ATF and local file released, any employee free to send records in, and retaliation made a crime. The statute is then audited line by line against this list.

The research behind Law 1. The Epstein Files Act passed 427 to 1 and still produced a fraction of its pages; the JFK Records Act left documents withheld thirty years past its deadline. Both failures are why this draft carries hard deadlines and criminal penalties.

A requirement-by-requirement audit of Law 1 against what citizens actually asked for, each one marked against the section that does the work. It also tracks what changed: ninety days became thirty, and presidential override was removed outright.

The demand behind Law 3 is different from disclosure. The concern is not only that files are withheld but that the case is reportedly not being worked, so the requirement is stated plainly: the FBI and the intelligence services must investigate.
The research behind Law 3 — the Special Counsel regulations and the Church Committee, read for one question only: how do you make investigative independence structural rather than merely promised?

The audit of Law 3 against the citizen requirements: a mandated investigation with its own team, budget and timeline, and a parallel intelligence assessment directed by the DNI. Every requirement is checked against the section that carries it.

The demand behind Law 4, in plain words: named public figures the audience actually trusts each get their own team inside the FBI and inside the intelligence community, and each picks who works on it.

The research behind Law 4. Special counsels are independent but still government appointees; the 9/11 Commission had subpoena power and classified access. This draft goes further, handing investigative authority to people outside government entirely.
The audit of Law 4: two teams per designated investigator, six in all, each with sole authority over who joins. Every citizen requirement is checked against the section that delivers it.
The plain-English demand behind Law 2: every part of the intelligence community — CIA, NSA, DIA, NRO — releases what it holds, and blocking an employee from coming forward becomes a crime.

The research behind Law 2, and its warning. The JFK Records Act ordered release in 1992 and agencies were still withholding in 2025. Intelligence disclosure laws fail on their exemptions, which is why this draft narrows protection to active sources only.
The audit of Law 2 against the citizen requirements: eight broad categories of covered information, a thirty-day catch-all mandate, and a final category built to cover whatever the list missed.

The build specification for the single slide that has to explain all four laws in one frame: 16:9, solid colours, no gradients, no imagery. It exists because the argument has to survive being screenshotted.

The slide specification for Law 2, matched to the Law 1 palette so the four read as one set. The frame has a single job: make plain that no agency file bearing on how Charlie Kirk was killed stays inside the building.
The slide specification for Law 3, in the same deep-navy, red and gold template as the rest. One message has to land in one frame: investigating this killing is a duty, not a choice.

The slide specification for Law 4, built to the same template as the other three. The frame has to make one idea legible at a glance — investigators the public actually trusts, working inside the agencies.
The launch article for all four laws in one place: why the Epstein Files Act is the model, and what each bill would force into daylight. Start here if you have never read the statutory text.

The charter document. All four bills summarised in order, with the agencies each one reaches and the case number they were drafted around. This is the file every compliance audit checks the drafts against.

An adversarial threat model of the laws' own weaknesses: every route by which the drafts could be slow-walked, narrowed or quietly ignored. Written so whoever has to close those holes can find them first.

The unfixed column of the fact-check. Nine of ten challenges were resolved and moved out; this page keeps the one that was not, a disclosure-item count that still has to be harmonised across the documents.

The attorney review of all four bills, with the vulnerabilities already closed — including the slow-rolling defence of producing records in a format nobody can search. Each item names the section that fixed it.

Twenty-six disclosure items proposed beyond the original list, all since folded into Schedule A of every bill. This is where family statements, witness-intimidation records and other late additions entered the text.

The fact-check that hardened the drafting. Every contested claim was reframed as a records request rather than an assertion, which is why the bills ask for all records relating to whether, instead of stating conclusions.

The attorney improvements already folded into Law 1: congressional findings for constitutional footing, a severability clause, and the rest of the structural work a bill needs to survive a challenge in court.

The compliance audit of all four drafts against the charter, with the resolved items kept on the record. Charter compliance is not academic: a bill has to survive contact with the agencies holding the files.
The archived March 2026 version of the Law 1 requirements, kept so the drafting history stays visible. Read beside the current page, it shows what citizens asked for and what the lawyers changed.
The archived legal-research notes for Law 1, preserved from the earlier draft. The precedents are the same; what changed is how much enforcement the drafters concluded was necessary.
The archived audit of the earlier Law 1 draft against the citizen requirements. Reading it beside the current version shows which gaps were closed, and when.
The original March 10, 2026 charter for the four bills, kept unchanged. The current summary supersedes it; this page is the record of where the project started.

An attorney's list of what would get these four bills struck down: the Schedule A item count differs across the drafts — 213, 214, 208, 208 — and naming seventeen private citizens as investigators runs straight at the Appointments Clause. It also flags the one authority no draft yet carries: an independent exhumation.

Every place the four drafts drift from their own charter, item by item: counts that do not match, a Definitions section buried behind Schedule A, and a required disclaimer Law 1 never carries. A charter is only worth something if somebody audits against it.
The archived earlier draft of Law 3, written while Schedule A still held 175 items. Read it beside the current text to see exactly what the attorney reviews changed.

The plain-English demand behind Law 3 as first written: disclosure alone is not enough, because an agency can hand over files and still decline to investigate. This is the archived version; the current one is here.

Precedent research for Law 3, kept as first drafted. The Special Counsel regulations, the Church Committee and the Warren Commission all read as one warning: a mandated investigation can still arrive at a predetermined conclusion.

The original audit of Law 3 against its own requirements, clause by clause. This is where the DNI-directed parallel intelligence assessment and the eight mandatory lead categories first appear in writing.

The archived first draft of Law 4, naming three trusted investigators where the current text names seventeen. Everything the later attorney review argued over — the Appointments Clause, the security detail, succession — starts here.

The demand in plain words before the lawyers touched it: give people the public actually trusts their own teams inside the FBI and inside the intelligence community, and make obstructing them a crime rather than a policy breach.

The precedent file for Law 4 as first assembled — special counsels, the 9/11 Commission, congressional clearance authority. The 9/11 Commission is the load-bearing example: private citizens holding subpoena power and classified access.
The original requirement-by-requirement audit of Law 4, every line marked MET with the section that meets it. Read it beside the current audit to see what the redraft added.

The archived earlier draft of the intelligence-community disclosure bill, back when Schedule A held 175 items. It already reached every element named in 50 U.S.C. 3003(4) — CIA, NSA, DIA, NRO, NGA, ODNI and the rest.

The plain-English demand behind Law 2 as first written: methods stay protected, conclusions do not. It also makes blocking a government employee from releasing that material a crime rather than a personnel matter.

Why Law 2 assumes bad faith. The JFK Records Act still left roughly five percent of records redacted after thirty years, and the Epstein Act produced about 12,285 documents against an estimated six million pages.

The original clause-by-clause audit of Law 2, showing where the catch-all beats the enumerated list. Section 1(b)(8) is the one that matters — a category built to cover whatever the other seven missed.

The most-cited medical-physics reading of the wound: a high-speed cavitation event, a snapped necklace, and an argument that a .30-06 carried far too much energy for what the video shows. The site notes his analysis reaches it secondhand, so checking it against his own posts is still an open task.

Eyewitness-level detail from inside the crowd: one razor-sharp bang like a firecracker, no echo, and a sound that seemed to rise upward rather than fall from a roof. Attributed claims from one account's threads, kept post by post rather than merged into a conclusion.

Where a verified kernel gets stacked with an unverified expansion. Joe Kent is on the record that his foreign-nexus inquiry was stopped; this account extends that to a second official who has said no such thing. The site marks exactly where the record ends.

The claim that a foreign newspaper confirmed Charlie Kirk's death before any American outlet did. Settling it needs the one thing nobody has published: a first-publication timestamp ledger with time zones and source desks attached.

A cabinet-level account quoted inside reply chains gave the 99-0404 overflight claim unusual reach. Hegseth himself connected nothing, and the site files the overflight sequence as unconfirmed pending ADS-B archives and FOIA returns.

Screenshots presented as Charlie's own private messages about donors and the pro-Israel cause. Either they are authentic and they bear directly on motive, or they are a case study in how unauthenticated text travels. Authentication is the open task, and nobody has done it.

Courtroom narration from the July 2026 preliminary hearing: an officer's body camera reportedly dying on the roof, a red-and-black screwdriver entered into evidence, and marks in the gravel described as a weapon rest. Summaries by a watcher, not a transcript.

One theory post, recorded as a theory: that the man who shouted "I shot him — now shoot me" was staging a diversion for someone else. He was detained and later cleared of the shooting itself, and no coordination has ever been shown.

TPUSA-critical commentary and hearing observations, including testimony that a roommate had never heard the accused mention Charlie Kirk before. The financial allegations riding alongside are unverified, and the site labels them that way rather than adopting them.

The official White House clip archive: a president urging revenge "at the voter box", a vice president crediting Kirk for his office, and a Justice Department pledge made in Charlie's name. This is the baseline the citizen investigation gets measured against.

Reposts that put the SUV-occupant questions into wide circulation — and a case study in restraint, because the compiler cropped the accusatory captions before publishing anything. The names attached to that seating chart remain unverified.

The scene-hardscaping question, amplified: ground material reportedly hauled away, then an "emergency directive" narrative about finishing by Monday. Work orders and directives are the records that would settle who ordered it and why.

A former state legislator who stood in the crowd, whose wide-angle photographs became primary records of the day, and who says he has met obstruction since. Every coincidence recorded about him is logged as a coincidence and nothing more.

Aviation analysis that cuts both ways: a "Task Force Charlie" command-relay theory with no tasking record behind it, alongside a technical argument that the airframe's trainer configuration could not launch or recover drones at all.

Citizen re-tellings of the July 2026 hearing, including the roof-timeline detail that feeds the shot clock. Its claim about a compromised roommate channel is attributed commentary the site records without adopting.

Image threads carrying the texts at the centre of the State's case, as they actually circulated. Useful for comparing the public versions against what was presented in court, where the phone testimony raised its own questions.

Scanner audio set against sworn testimony: an officer heard calling in a rooftop imprint but not a screwdriver or a casing, and a dispatch call said to be missing from circulated archives. The site stresses this is not a finding of perjury.

The clip library for the exploding-mic and second-actor lanes: witness statements describing a chest wound, a man in all black leaving the scene, and the shirt-pull observation. Reposted material, attributed rather than asserted.

A broadcast promo claiming, six days in, that "they knew beforehand" — the earliest high-reach prior-knowledge framing in the case. The site logs it as a narrative marker needing primary sourcing, not as reporting.

One viral post compressed the whole exploding-mic stack into a single sequence: a defense contract, a device under the shirt, then an explosives plant destroyed a month later. Skeptics answer that explosives factories explode without conspiracy.

A cartoon and a slide video showing how the drone and intelligence questions travelled visually. The final slide carries the author's own disclaimer, which the site treats as governing: no claim is made that a drone assassinated anyone.

A single annotated screenshot, widely viewed: two circles drawn on a man being escorted across pavement. The site's own assessment is blunt — a rear-pocket bulge in a compressed screenshot is not evidence of anything specific.

A clip-sharing account whose contribution is source circulation: the declassified MK-Ultra background material that frames, but never proves, the conditioning theories some researchers try to apply to this case.

The "two patsies" reading in its sharpest form, mapped rather than endorsed. One man's obstruction is court record; whether it was coordinated with anything is not, and nobody here is found to have taken part in a crime.

July 2026 clips that moved wound-geometry arguments out of long-form video and onto X. The underlying autopsy measurements are not public, which keeps every trajectory claim second-hand analysis rather than proof.

A foreign state broadcaster amplifying Charlie's Israel-critical clips at scale. The site uses its posts only as evidence of what circulated and when, checking quote context against the primary videos rather than the outlet's framing.

The only claimed inside-the-room account of the foreign lane closing: two unnamed sources said to have sat in a cabinet meeting six days after the killing. Anonymous, secondhand, and graded the weakest of three strands.

The September 2025 four-actor "distraction" roster that other accounts then reused as a template. None of those detained has been found by any court to have aided a shooter, which is exactly why it stays a taxonomy.

Among the first accounts to broadcast the father-assisted turn-in, which fixed the public chronology of the surrender inside forty-eight hours. That baseline is what every later custody-timeline argument measures against.

Frame-by-frame composites catalogued objects sitting on a surface that was excavated and paved over four days later. Crushed water bottles under a shoe now survive only in photographs, which is the whole point.

The account that published a contractor's on-camera account of being told the courtyard had to be finished by Monday, alongside clips of conservative media fighting over whether citizen investigation is legitimate at all.

A first-party corporate account rather than a citizen investigator: two posts, deleted within hours, naming a different firm as TPUSA's contracted security on September 10. The corporate registration behind them is public record and checkable.
The clearest technical explainer of the most over-read word in this case. "Inconclusive" means the ATF neither identified nor excluded the seized rifle — not an exclusion, and not a match.

Court-watch coverage of the paper war: a discovery stall over DNA chain-of-custody records, a continuance granted over objection, and a contempt finding against a prosecutor. Commentary on filings, not the filings themselves.

The camera behind Charlie's head faced both the wound and the rooftop line, and its card reportedly left the scene within five minutes. Who took it and where it went are precise, answerable chain-of-custody questions.

The strongest form of the coordination reading of the "shoot me" outburst, kept next to the official position that the obstruction was real but uncoordinated. Documented as framing, never as a finding.
One misread timestamp reached tens of millions of views: a Dairy Queen still read as minutes after the shot rather than six hours later. A case study in how public clocks mutate in the retelling.

The most-shared geometric argument against the rooftop account — an entry at C2 the poster calls mathematically impossible from that roof at that range. It can only be tested against autopsy measurements that remain sealed.

Within hours of the shooting, a private jet leaving Provo and dropping off ADS-B became the first aircraft thread of the case. The dropout is checkable; terrain shadowing and blocked tail numbers are the ordinary explanations.
The most sustained scrutiny of the custody clock: an on-camera Miranda warning at 6:25 PM against a Discord confession stamped 7:57 PM. Narrow, testable, and aimed at documents rather than motives.

Alternative-mechanism theories with real reach: an infrared reflection on a phone screen, a casing rolling down the tent tarp, and hinged hardware that fires around a corner. Opinion media — no such weapon is in evidence.
